newsitem.title: USA: Death sentence upheld for Fla. student slayer.
newsitem.headline: Death sentence upheld for Fla. student slayer.

text.p: The Florida Supreme Court Thursday upheld the death sentences of Danny Rolling, convicted for the macabre 1990 serial murders of five college students that sent panic through the University of Florida.

Rolling, who pleaded guilty to the murders on the first day of his 1991 trial, faces death in Florida's electric chair for a four-day killing spree that left four women and a man dead and led to a frenzied search for their killer.

The crimes were among the most brutal in Florida history. Three victims were raped, one was beheaded and police said the killer had bound and gagged some of his victims and described how he planned to torture them.

Rolling's attorneys argued to the state high court that the trial should have been moved from Gainesville, site of the University of Florida, because it was impossible to find jurors who had not heard of the case.
After striking down each argument in Rolling's appeal, the high court took the unusual step of reiterating its support for the death penalty in each of the slayings.

"Our review of the entire record in this case shows that death is the appropriate sentence in each of these brutal murders and is not disproportionate given the facts of this case," the court concluded in a 19-page ruling.

Rolling, a career criminal and the son of a retired Shreveport, La., police officer, began the killing spree in the early morning hours of Aug. 24, 1990, when he broke into the apartment of students Sonya Larson and Christina Powell.
After stabbing Larson to death, Rolling attacked Powell, sexually abused her and stabbed her to death.

After the killings, Rolling took the bodies and arranged them in the apartment, posing them in positions apparently intended to shock whoever discovered them. In one instance a woman's severed head was placed on a stereo turntable, according to published reports.
Two days later, Rolling killed again, lying in wait for Christa Hoyt, who was killed shortly before noon after being sexually abused. Her body, too, was posed after she died.
A day later, Rolling broke into the apartment of college students Tracy Paules and Manuel Taboada. After stabbing Taboada to death, Rolling stalked, raped and killed Paules, again posing her body.
The killing spree created a panic at the University of Florida campus. Hundreds of students left the school. Others took to carrying mace and other weapons.
At a Gainesville news conference, State Attorney Rod Smith said he was pleased the court had affirmed the decision to hold Rolling's trial in the town where the murders took place.
"It was a strategy on Rolling's part to be tried in Gainesville and then complain about it later," Smith said.
A statement from the victims' families said they were frustrated the case had taken three years to get to this point but happy "that Rolling is moving closer to his execution."
"You never have complete closure, you always miss your children," said Anna Hoyt, mother of victim Christa Hoyt. "We don't get an appeal. There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Christa."
